titre: Barter, the Supposed Origin of Money
accroche: In 1985, Caroline Humphrey notes that no pure barter economy has ever been described. So where does the story of money born from barter come from?
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1776, in The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith imagines a butcher who has more meat than he can consume. The brewer and the baker would gladly buy some, but they have nothing to offer him except the products of their own trades, and the butcher already has all the bread and beer he needs: “no exchange can, in this case, take place between them,” Smith writes. Out of this impasse he derives money, a good that everyone accepts in order to unblock what direct exchange cannot settle. The story, repeated since in many economics textbooks, tells of a humanity that supposedly went through a stage of barter before inventing money.

## A story short on fieldwork

In 1985, in Man, the anthropologist Caroline Humphrey rejects what her abstract calls the view of mainstream economists: barter as a “natural” phenomenon of human nature and as the origin of money. Her article opens with a finding: no example of a pure and simple barter economy has ever been described, let alone the emergence of money out of such an economy; all the available ethnography suggests that no such thing ever existed. The next sentence is a qualification: there are economies today in which barter dominates. The finding therefore concerns the imagined primitive stage, not barter itself.

## Barter exists, but under specific conditions

Humphrey shows that barter occurs under particular socioeconomic conditions, which can also be found in economies that know money: when the money supply is very low, money can cease to serve as a standard of value and become itself an object of barter; barter is also likely when small social groups want to preserve their autonomy. Drawing on the case of the Lhomi, in northeastern Nepal, she describes a barter that tends to be practiced among people who know each other, because only the fixing of customary times and places of exchange spares them the costs of searching for partners and waiting. In other words, the barter we observe is not the state of affairs before money.

David Graeber extends this critique in Debt: The First 5,000 Years (2011), whose reference page presents the central thesis: debt came before money, and credit systems are older than coins. In his review, the economist Suresh Naidu sums up the thesis this way: money does not come from a “natural” propensity to barter, but from an institutional construction that relies on the quantification of gift relations that Graeber calls “debt.” Naidu adds that the book speculates and provokes more than it proves, and that the evidence is never watertight.

The thesis remains debated. The economist Robert Murphy responds on September 1, 2011, to an interview Graeber gave to the blog Naked Capitalism, not to the book itself. In his view, the phase of pure barter would be brief, with indirect exchange setting in almost immediately; so the fact that no barter economies are found is not enough, in his eyes, to rule out the classical explanation. That is the shift: the origin of money is argued between a logical deduction and observations, and Humphrey reminds us that the first is no substitute for the second.

quiz.question: What does the anthropologist Caroline Humphrey note in 1985 about barter?
choix: That barter came before money in every society studied
That barter is now the norm in most rural economies
That no pure barter economy has been described, nor the emergence of money from one
That money and barter appeared at the same time in all societies
quiz.explication: Humphrey writes that no example of a pure and simple barter economy has been described, nor the emergence of money from one, while noting that barter-dominated economies exist today. She does not say that barter preceded money everywhere, that it is the current norm, or that the two appeared together.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Adam Smith's example of the butcher, the brewer, and the baker show?
choix: That the butcher systematically refused any exchange with the brewer
That barter between craftsmen of the same village worked better than between strangers
That money supposedly appeared in England before barter, unlike in the rest of the world
That without money, the butcher and those who would like his meat cannot trade
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In Smith, the brewer and the baker would like to buy meat but have only the products of their own trades to offer, which the butcher already has: without money, no exchange takes place, which is what money would come to solve.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what conditions does Caroline Humphrey place the barter she studies among the Lhomi of Nepal?
choix: When the money supply is very low or small groups want to preserve their autonomy
Only in societies that have never known money in any form
Between totally anonymous strangers who will never see each other again
At the large trade fairs of medieval Europe
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Humphrey places barter in particular socioeconomic conditions, which can also exist in economies that know money: a very low money supply, or small groups' desire to maintain their autonomy. Among the Lhomi, it tends to be practiced between people who know each other.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the economist Robert Murphy responding to in his text of September 1, 2011?
choix: The Mesopotamian archaeological data cited in Graeber's book
An interview Graeber gave to the blog Naked Capitalism, not the book itself
The fieldwork methodology Caroline Humphrey used among the Lhomi
The chapter on ancient Greece in Graeber's book
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Murphy responds to an interview with Graeber published on Naked Capitalism the previous week, in order to defend the classical explanation; he does not draw on the argument developed in the book.
